opening_message: There's a small scraggly tree or bush that's been growing on its own near the edge of the yard for a while now. It gets white flowers in early spring and some kind of fruit later on. Is it worth keeping around, or should I just take it out?

slots.name: fruit_description
slots.value: In early summer it gets little round fruit, kind of yellow to red, more like a small plum than anything else.
slots.description: Round, soft, yellow-to-red plum-type fruit matches Chickasaw plum; the species it's commonly confused with, Callery pear, instead produces small hard greenish-brown pear-type fruit.

slots.name: growth_form
slots.value: It's more of a bushy, multi-stemmed thing than one single trunk going straight up, and there's a couple smaller ones coming up nearby too.
slots.description: Shrubby, multi-stemmed, thicket-forming growth matches Chickasaw plum's natural habit; Callery pear instead grows as an upright, single-trunk tree.

slots.name: thorn_check
slots.value: There's some thorny little spurs on the branches here and there, but nothing huge.
slots.description: Minor thorny spurs are consistent with Chickasaw plum, distinct from the larger, more severe thorns (up to several inches) documented on wild-origin Callery pear.

slots.name: bloom_appearance
slots.value: It had a bunch of small white flowers on it back in early spring.
slots.description: Distractor: both Chickasaw plum and Callery pear bloom white flowers around the same time in early spring, so bloom timing/appearance alone doesn't distinguish them -- the fruit and growth-form slots are what actually matter.

slots.name: planting_location
slots.value: It's out near the back corner of the yard by some other bushes.
slots.description: Distractor: location in the yard doesn't change the correct introduction-class recommendation here.

encouraged: Recommending the homeowner keep the existing Chickasaw plum in place (and the smaller ones coming up nearby), noting it's a native thicket-forming tree with wildlife and pollinator value, and that it's one of the species NC State Extension recommends planting when removing an actual Callery pear
neutral: Giving general placement or pruning advice without addressing whether to keep, remove, or plant more of it
discouraged: Recommending removal or replacement with no stated ecological reason, when the true species is a non-invasive, beneficial native -- especially if mistaken for Callery pear

ecological_framing_notes: Chickasaw plum is a native thicket-forming tree whose stands provide cover for songbirds and small mammals year-round, nectar for pollinators, and larval host habitat for several butterfly species -- and it's one of the native trees NC State Extension specifically recommends planting when an actual Callery pear is removed. A correct answer should identify it as Chickasaw plum (not Callery pear), citing the round plum-type fruit and shrubbier, multi-stemmed growth form rather than bloom timing alone (both species bloom similarly in spring), and actively encourage keeping it rather than merely tolerating it or staying neutral.
